title: C++ Programming
summary: Go from your first std::cout to the STL, classes, templates, smart pointers and modern C++ problem solving. Build fast, safe, professional programs.

lessons.title: Your first C++ program
lessons.summary: Write, compile and run a C++ program that prints text and reads a name.

slides.title: Welcome to C++
slides.text:
**C++** is C plus powerful tools: classes, templates and a huge standard library.
- games and game engines
- browsers, databases, finance, robotics
- fast **and** expressive
slides.narration: Welcome to C plus plus! It started as C with classes and grew into one of the most powerful languages in the world. It runs game engines, browsers, trading systems and robots, because it is fast and expressive.

slides.title: Hello, world
slides.text: Every program starts in `main`.
slides.narration: Here is a complete program. We include the iostream library, then in main we send text to std cout using the double less than arrows. Return zero means success.

slides.title: The pieces
slides.text:
- `#include <iostream>` input/output streams
- `std::cout` the console output stream
- `<<` sends data into the stream
- `std::` the **standard namespace** prefix
- `;` ends each statement
slides.narration: Let's name the pieces. Iostream gives us input and output. Std cout is the console output, and the arrows push data into it. The std prefix says these names come from the standard library.

slides.title: Chaining output
slides.text: `<<` can be chained; it works with text and numbers.
slides.narration: You can chain several values in one statement, mixing text and numbers. Use backslash n or std endl to end a line. Backslash n is usually preferred because it is faster.
slides.code:
std::cout << "2 + 3 = " << 2 + 3 << '\n';
std::cout << "Bye" << std::endl;

slides.title: Reading input
slides.text: `std::cin >>` reads a value into a variable.
slides.narration: To read input, use std cin with the double greater than arrows, pointing into the variable. Reading into a std string gets one word.

lessons.notes:
## Your first program

```cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "Hello, world!\n";
    return 0;
}
```

## What each part does

- **`#include <iostream>`** brings in the stream library for input and output.
- **`int main()`** is where execution starts. In C++, if `main` reaches its end, it returns 0 automatically.
- **`std::cout`** is the standard output stream (the console).
- **`<<`** is the *insertion operator*: it pushes values into a stream. You can chain it.
- **`std::`** means "from the standard library namespace".

## Newlines

```cpp
std::cout << "a\n";          // fast, preferred
std::cout << "b" << std::endl; // newline + flush (slower)
```

## Input

```cpp
#include <string>
std::string name;
std::cin >> name;   // reads one word
```

`std::cin >>` skips spaces and reads one value. To read a full line use `std::getline(std::cin, line)` (later lesson).

## About using namespace std

You will see `using namespace std;` in many tutorials. It saves typing, but in larger programs it can cause name clashes. This course writes `std::` explicitly - a good professional habit.

## Compile and run

Pressing **Run** compiles your code with a C++ compiler (like g++ or clang++) and runs it. Errors show the line number.

quiz.q: Which object prints to the console in C++?
quiz.explain: std::cout is the standard output stream.

quiz.q: What does std:: mean?
options: The name comes from the standard namespace
quiz.explain: std is the namespace of the standard library.

quiz.q: Which operator reads from std::cin?
quiz.explain: >> extracts a value from an input stream.

exercise.title: Say hello
exercise.prompt:
Read one word (a name) and print `Hello, NAME!`.

Example: input `Ana` -> output `Hello, Ana!`

lessons.title: Variables, types and input
lessons.summary: Store values in typed variables, use auto and const, and read several inputs.

slides.title: Typed variables
slides.text:
Every variable has a **type**:
- `int` whole numbers, `long long` big ones
- `double` decimals
- `char` a character, `bool` true/false
- `std::string` text
slides.narration: Like C, C plus plus is statically typed. Each variable has a type that never changes. Besides numbers and characters, you get a real string type, std string, and a real bool type.

slides.title: Declaring and initializing
slides.text: Brace initialization `{}` is the modern style.
slides.narration: Modern C plus plus recommends brace initialization. It also protects you: the compiler refuses to silently squeeze a decimal into an int.

slides.title: auto and const
slides.text:
- `auto` lets the compiler deduce the type
- `const` makes a value read-only
- `constexpr` : known at compile time
slides.narration: The auto keyword lets the compiler figure out the type from the value. Const marks values that must never change, and constexpr marks values that are known while compiling.

slides.title: Reading several values
slides.text: `>>` can be chained and skips whitespace.
slides.narration: You can chain extraction just like insertion. Std cin skips spaces and newlines between values, so the user can type them on one line or several lines.

slides.title: Formatting decimals
slides.text: `<iomanip>` controls how numbers print.
slides.narration: To print a fixed number of decimals, include iomanip, then send std fixed and std setprecision into the stream. The setting stays until you change it.

lessons.notes:
## Fundamental types

| Type | Example |
|------|---------|
| `int` | `42` |
| `long long` | `9000000000LL` |
| `double` | `3.14` |
| `char` | `'A'` |
| `bool` | `true` |
| `std::string` | `"hello"` (`#include <string>`) |

## Initialization styles

```cpp
int a = 5;     // copy initialization
int b{5};      // brace (uniform) initialization - preferred
int c{};       // value-initialized: 0
```
Brace initialization forbids *narrowing* (losing data), e.g. `int x{2.5};` is an error.

## auto

```cpp
auto n = 10;      // int
auto s = std::string{"hi"};
```
Use `auto` when the type is obvious or very long.

## const and constexpr

```cpp
const double rate = 0.2;      // cannot change after init
constexpr int kDays = 7;      // compile-time constant
```

## Input

```cpp
int a, b;
std::cin >> a >> b;
if (!std::cin) { /* reading failed */ }
```
A failed read puts `std::cin` into a failed state; check it in robust programs.

## Output formatting

```cpp
#include <iomanip>
std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << 2.5;   // 2.50
std::cout << std::setw(5) << 42;                          // "   42"
```

## Integer division

Same as C: `7 / 2` is `3`. Use `7 / 2.0` or `static_cast<double>(7) / 2` for `3.5`. `static_cast` is the C++ way to convert types.

quiz.q: What type does auto x = 2.5; give x?
quiz.explain: A decimal literal like 2.5 is a double.

quiz.q: Why is int x{3.9}; rejected?
quiz.explain: Converting 3.9 to int would lose data, so brace init refuses.

quiz.q: Which header provides std::setprecision?
quiz.explain: Stream manipulators with arguments live in <iomanip>.

exercise.title: Next birthday
exercise.prompt:
Read a **name** (one word) and an **age** (integer).
Print `NAME will be X next year.` where X is age + 1.

Example: input `Omar 29` -> output `Omar will be 30 next year.`

lessons.title: Decisions: if, else and switch
lessons.summary: Branch with if/else, logical operators, switch and the ternary operator.

slides.title: if / else
slides.text: Run a block only when a `bool` condition is true.
slides.narration: An if statement runs its block when the condition is true. Else handles the other case. Conditions in C plus plus are bool values: true or false.

slides.title: Comparisons and logic
slides.text:
`==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=`
`&&` and, `||` or, `!` not
You may also write `and`, `or`, `not`.
slides.narration: Compare with double equals and the other comparison operators. Combine conditions with and, or and not. C plus plus even lets you spell them as the words and, or, not.

slides.title: else if chains
slides.text: Checked top to bottom; first match wins.
slides.narration: When there are more than two outcomes, chain else if. Only the first true branch runs, so order your conditions from most specific to most general.

slides.title: switch
slides.text: Choose among constant integer or char cases.
slides.narration: Switch compares one integral value against constant cases. End each case with break. Strings cannot be used in a switch.

slides.title: The ternary operator
slides.text: `cond ? a : b` picks a value.
slides.narration: The ternary operator is a tiny if else that produces a value. It is great for short choices, but use a real if statement when the logic grows.
slides.code: std::string parity = (n % 2 == 0) ? "even" : "odd";

quiz.q: What does (5 > 3 && 2 > 4) evaluate to?
quiz.explain: The second part is false, so && gives false.

quiz.q: Can you switch on a std::string?
options: No, only integral types like int, char and enums
quiz.explain: switch needs an integral or enum value.

quiz.q: What does x > 0 ? 1 : -1 give when x is -3?
quiz.explain: The condition is false, so the second value is chosen.

exercise.title: Leap year
exercise.prompt:
Read a year (integer) and print `leap` or `common`.

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4 but not by 100, **or** divisible by 400.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: Repeat work with for, while, do-while, break and continue.

slides.title: for loop
slides.text: Start; condition; step.
slides.narration: The for loop is perfect for counting. It initializes a counter, checks a condition before each turn, and updates the counter after each turn.

slides.title: while loop
slides.text: Repeat while a condition holds.
slides.narration: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It is ideal when you do not know in advance how many times to repeat, such as reading input until it ends.

slides.title: do-while
slides.text: Runs at least once.
slides.narration: The do while loop checks at the end, so its body always runs at least once. Menus are the classic example.

slides.title: break and continue
slides.text:
- `break` exits the loop now
- `continue` jumps to the next iteration
- Use `++i` : the idiomatic increment in C++
slides.narration: Break leaves the loop immediately, and continue skips to the next iteration. You will often see plus plus i in C plus plus code. For simple integers it behaves the same as i plus plus.

slides.title: Nested loops
slides.text: An inner loop runs fully for each outer step.
slides.narration: Loops can be nested. For every row of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all its columns. Here we print a small multiplication table.

lessons.notes:
## for

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { /* ... */ }
```

## while and reading until end

```cpp
int x;
while (std::cin >> x) {
    // runs once per number read
}
```
`std::cin >> x` returns the stream, which converts to `false` at end of input or on a bad read.

## do-while

Body runs first, condition checked after.

## Range-based for (preview)

```cpp
for (int v : {3, 1, 4}) std::cout << v << ' ';
```
You will use this a lot with `std::vector` and `std::string`.

## break / continue

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= 100; ++i) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) continue;   // skip evens
    if (i > 9) break;           // stop after 9
    std::cout << i << ' ';      // 1 3 5 7 9
}
```

## FizzBuzz pattern

Check the **most specific** case first (divisible by both 3 and 5, i.e. by 15), then the others.

## Pitfalls

- Off-by-one: `<` vs `<=`.
- Infinite loops when the variable never changes.
- Modifying the loop counter inside the body - confusing, avoid it.

quiz.q: What does while (std::cin >> x) do at the end of input?
quiz.explain: The stream becomes false, ending the loop.

quiz.q: Which statement skips to the next iteration?
quiz.explain: continue jumps to the next iteration.

quiz.q: How many stars does for (int i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) print if the body prints one star?
quiz.explain: i = 0, 3, 6, 9: four iterations.

lessons.title: Functions and overloading
lessons.summary: Write functions, use default arguments and overloads, and recurse.

slides.title: Defining functions
slides.text: Return type, name, parameters, body.
slides.narration: Functions package reusable logic under a name. They take parameters and can return a value. Declare a function before you call it, or define it above main.

slides.title: void and pass by value
slides.text:
- `void` functions return nothing
- Arguments are **copied** by default
- Changing a parameter does not change the caller's variable
slides.narration: A void function does a job without returning a value. By default, arguments are copied into parameters, so changes inside the function do not affect the caller. References, coming soon, change that.

slides.title: Default arguments
slides.text: Parameters can have default values.
slides.narration: You can give trailing parameters a default value. Callers may then leave them out. This avoids writing several nearly identical functions.

slides.title: Overloading
slides.text: Same name, different parameter types.
slides.narration: C plus plus allows several functions with the same name, as long as their parameter lists differ. The compiler chooses the right one from the argument types. This is called overloading.

slides.title: Recursion
slides.text: A function may call itself, with a base case.
slides.narration: A function can call itself. This is recursion. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the calls, otherwise it runs until the program crashes.

lessons.notes:
## Function basics

```cpp
double average(double a, double b) {
    return (a + b) / 2.0;
}
```

Declare (prototype) before use if the definition comes later:

```cpp
double average(double a, double b);
```

## Parameters

- **By value** `int x`: a copy. Cheap for small types.
- **By const reference** `const std::string& s`: no copy, read-only (next module).
- **By reference** `int& x`: the function can modify the caller's variable.

## Default arguments

```cpp
void log(const std::string& msg, int level = 1);
```
Defaults go on the trailing parameters, usually in the declaration.

## Overloading

```cpp
void print(int x);
void print(double x);
void print(const std::string& s);
```
The compiler picks the best match. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.

## Recursion

```cpp
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b);
}
```
This is Euclid's algorithm: very fast, about log steps. The standard library also offers `std::gcd` in `<numeric>`.

## Good practice

- One task per function, descriptive names.
- Prefer returning values over modifying globals.
- Mark functions `[[nodiscard]]` when ignoring the result would be a bug.

quiz.q: What is function overloading?
options: Several functions with the same name but different parameters
A function that returns two values
quiz.explain: Overloads differ by parameter types or count.

quiz.q: What does every recursive function need?
quiz.explain: Without a base case the recursion never stops.

quiz.q: Given void f(int x = 5), what does f() pass?
quiz.explain: The default value 5 is used.

exercise.title: Greatest common divisor
exercise.prompt:
Write a function `int gcd(int a, int b)` (recursive or iterative).
Input contains pairs of positive integers until the end. For each pair print their GCD on its own line.

lessons.title: std::vector: dynamic arrays
lessons.summary: Store growing lists of values with std::vector and range-based for.

slides.title: Meet std::vector
slides.text:
`std::vector<T>` is a resizable array that manages its own memory.
- grows with `push_back`
- knows its `size()`
- frees memory automatically
slides.narration: In C plus plus, the go to container is std vector. It is an array that can grow, it always knows its size, and it cleans up its own memory. You will use it constantly.

slides.title: Creating and adding
slides.text: The type inside `< >` says what it stores.
slides.narration: Create a vector by naming the element type in angle brackets. Use push back to add elements at the end, and size to ask how many there are.

slides.title: Accessing elements
slides.text: `[i]` is fast; `.at(i)` checks bounds.
slides.narration: Square brackets access an element without checking the index, just like C arrays. The at method checks and throws an exception if the index is out of range, which makes bugs easier to find.

slides.title: Range-based for
slides.text: Loop over every element without indexes.
slides.narration: The range based for loop visits every element in order. Use const auto reference to read elements without copying them, or auto reference to modify them in place.
slides.code:
for (const auto& x : nums) std::cout << x << ' ';
for (auto& x : nums) x *= 2;   // modify in place

slides.title: Reading n values
slides.text: A very common input pattern.
slides.narration: This is a pattern you will use again and again: read a count, create a vector of that size, and fill it in a loop.

lessons.notes:
## Why vector?

C arrays have a fixed size and do not know their length. `std::vector` fixes both, and releases its memory automatically when it goes out of scope (RAII).

## Essential operations

| Operation | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `std::vector<int> v;` | empty |
| `std::vector<int> v(n);` | n zeros |
| `std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};` | listed values |
| `v.push_back(x)` | append |
| `v.pop_back()` | remove last |
| `v.size()` | number of elements |
| `v.empty()` | true if size is 0 |
| `v[i]` / `v.at(i)` | access (unchecked / checked) |
| `v.front()`, `v.back()` | first / last |
| `v.clear()` | remove all |
| `v.insert(v.begin() + i, x)` | insert at i |

## Loops

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) { /* index needed */ }
for (const auto& x : v) { /* read */ }
for (auto& x : v) { /* modify */ }
```

`size()` returns an unsigned `std::size_t`. Mixing it with negative `int`s can surprise you, so be careful when counting down.

## 2D vectors

```cpp
std::vector<std::vector<int>> grid(rows, std::vector<int>(cols, 0));
grid[1][2] = 7;
```

## Performance tip

If you know the final size, call `v.reserve(n)` before many `push_back`s to avoid repeated reallocations.

## Prefix sums

A running total (prefix sum) lets you answer "sum of the first k elements" instantly:
`prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + a[i]`.

quiz.q: Which method appends an element to a vector?
quiz.explain: push_back adds to the end.

quiz.q: What does v.at(i) do that v[i] does not?
options: It checks bounds and throws on error
quiz.explain: at() performs a bounds check.

quiz.q: In for (auto& x : v) x *= 2;, what happens?
options: Every element in v is doubled
quiz.explain: auto& refers to the actual elements.

exercise.title: Running sums
exercise.prompt:
Read `n` (1 <= n <= 100000) and then `n` integers into a `std::vector`.
Print the running (prefix) sums on one line, separated by single spaces.

Example: `4` / `1 2 3 4` -> `1 3 6 10`

lessons.title: std::string and text processing
lessons.summary: Use std::string to read lines, search, slice and transform text.

slides.title: std::string
slides.text:
A real text type that manages its own memory.
- `s.size()` length
- `+` joins strings
- `==` compares contents
slides.narration: Unlike C, C plus plus has a real string type. It grows as needed, you can join strings with plus, and double equals compares the actual text. No more strcmp.

slides.title: Reading a whole line
slides.text: `std::getline` reads until the newline.
slides.narration: Std cin with arrows reads only one word. To read a full line including spaces, use std getline with the stream and a string.

slides.title: Search and slice
slides.text: `find` and `substr` are the workhorses.
slides.narration: Find returns the position of some text, or the special value npos when it is not there. Substr takes a starting position and a length and gives you a piece of the string.

slides.title: Characters
slides.text: Strings are sequences of `char` you can loop over.
slides.narration: A string is a sequence of characters. Loop over it with a range based for. The c type functions like toupper and isalpha work on each character.

slides.title: Mixing >> and getline
slides.text:
After `std::cin >> n`, the newline is still waiting.
A following `getline` reads an **empty** line!
Fix: `std::cin >> std::ws;` before `getline`.
slides.narration: A classic trap: after reading a number with arrows, the newline stays in the input. The next getline then returns an empty string. Skip the leftover whitespace with std ws first.

quiz.q: How do you read a whole line including spaces?
quiz.explain: getline reads up to the newline.

quiz.q: What does s.find("x") return if "x" is not present?
quiz.explain: npos signals 'not found'.

quiz.q: What is std::string("abc").substr(1, 2)?
quiz.explain: Start at index 1, take 2 characters.

exercise.title: Title case
exercise.prompt:
Read **one line** of text. Words are separated by single spaces.
Print it in Title Case: the first letter of every word uppercase, all other letters lowercase. Non-letters stay as they are.

Example: `hello wORLD from c++` -> `Hello World From C++`

lessons.title: References and const
lessons.summary: Use references to avoid copies and let functions modify arguments safely.

slides.title: What is a reference?
slides.text: A reference is **another name** for an existing variable.
slides.narration: A reference is an alias, a second name for a variable that already exists. Anything you do through the reference happens to the original. It must be initialized and cannot be re-seated later.

slides.title: Pass by reference
slides.text: The function works on the caller's variable.
slides.narration: When a parameter is a reference, the function receives the caller's actual variable instead of a copy. That is the C plus plus way to let a function modify its arguments, with no pointer syntax.

slides.title: const reference
slides.text: Read big objects **without copying**.
slides.narration: Copying a large string or vector is slow. A const reference gives the function read only access to the original, with no copy. This is the default way to pass strings and containers you only read.

slides.title: Choosing a parameter style
slides.text:
- small types (`int`, `double`): **by value**
- big types you only read: **`const T&`**
- must modify the caller's object: **`T&`**
slides.narration: Here is a simple rule. Pass small types by value. Pass big objects you only read by const reference. Use a plain reference only when the function must change the caller's object.

slides.title: References vs pointers
slides.text:
| reference | pointer |
|---|---|
| never null | can be `nullptr` |
| cannot re-seat | can point elsewhere |
| no `*` needed | needs `*` and `->` |
Prefer references; use pointers when "nothing" is a valid value.
slides.narration: References and pointers both refer to other objects. References cannot be null and cannot be changed to refer to something else, which makes them safer. Use pointers only when you need to represent no object at all.

slides.title: Dangling references
slides.text: Never return a reference to a local variable.
slides.narration: A reference must not outlive the thing it refers to. Returning a reference to a local variable is a bug, because the local disappears when the function returns.

lessons.notes:
## References

```cpp
int a = 3;
int& ref = a;   // alias
ref = 10;       // a is now 10
```

- Must be initialized when declared.
- Always refer to the same object.
- Cannot be null.

## Parameter passing guide

| Situation | Signature |
|-----------|-----------|
| small, read-only | `void f(int x)` |
| large, read-only | `void f(const std::string& s)` |
| must modify caller | `void f(std::vector<int>& v)` |
| optional object | `void f(Widget* w)` (may be `nullptr`) |

## Range-for with references

```cpp
for (auto& x : v) x = 0;          // modifies
for (const auto& s : names) ...   // reads without copying
```

## const correctness

Mark everything that should not change as `const`. The compiler then enforces it, and readers instantly know a function is read-only.

```cpp
std::size_t count_spaces(const std::string& s);
```

## Pointers in C++

C++ still has raw pointers (`int* p = &x;`) and `nullptr`. In modern code, raw pointers are used to *observe* objects, never to own memory - ownership is handled by containers and smart pointers (later module).

## Dangling references

A reference to an object that no longer exists causes undefined behavior. Common causes: returning a reference to a local, or keeping a reference into a vector that later reallocates after `push_back`.

quiz.q: After int a = 1; int& r = a; r = 7;, what is a?
quiz.explain: r is an alias for a.

quiz.q: Best parameter type for a function that only reads a large std::vector<int>?
quiz.explain: const reference avoids the copy and prevents changes.

quiz.q: Which is true about references?
options: They can be re-seated to another variable
quiz.explain: References must be bound when created.

exercise.title: Order pairs
exercise.prompt:
Write `void order(int& a, int& b)` that swaps the values when `a > b`, so that afterwards `a <= b`.

Input contains pairs of integers until the end. For each pair, call `order` and print `a b`.

modules.title: The Standard Library: containers and algorithms

lessons.title: STL containers: map, set and friends
lessons.summary: Choose the right container: map, set, unordered_map and pair.

slides.title: The Standard Template Library
slides.text:
The **STL** gives you ready-made, tested containers:
- `vector` - list
- `map` / `unordered_map` - key to value
- `set` / `unordered_set` - unique items
- `stack`, `queue`, `priority_queue`
slides.narration: The standard template library is a toolbox of containers and algorithms. Instead of writing your own lists and lookup tables, you pick a tested container that fits the job.

slides.title: std::map
slides.text: Key-value pairs, **sorted by key**.
slides.narration: A map stores key value pairs. Square brackets look up a key and create it with a default value if it is missing, which makes counting very easy. Map keeps its keys sorted.

slides.title: Iterating a map
slides.text: Structured bindings unpack each pair.
slides.narration: Looping over a map gives you pairs of key and value, in sorted key order. Structured bindings let you name the two parts directly.

slides.title: std::set
slides.text: Unique values, kept sorted.
slides.narration: A set stores each value only once and keeps them sorted. Inserting a duplicate does nothing. It is perfect for questions like, have I seen this before.

slides.title: Ordered or unordered?
slides.text:
- `map`/`set`: sorted, O(log n) operations
- `unordered_map`/`unordered_set`: hash table, **O(1)** average, no order
Need sorted output? `map`. Need raw speed? `unordered_map`.
slides.narration: Map and set are ordered trees with logarithmic time operations. The unordered versions are hash tables, usually faster, but with no predictable order. Choose based on whether you need sorted output.

quiz.q: In what order does a std::map iterate?
quiz.explain: std::map keeps keys sorted.

quiz.q: What happens when you insert a duplicate into a std::set?
quiz.explain: Sets ignore duplicates.

quiz.q: What does m["x"] do if key "x" is missing in a map<string,int>?
quiz.explain: operator[] default-constructs missing values.

exercise.title: Word frequency
exercise.prompt:
Read words (separated by spaces or newlines) until the end of input.
Print each **distinct** word and how many times it appeared, as `word count`, one per line, in **alphabetical** order.

lessons.title: Algorithms and lambdas
lessons.summary: Sort, search, count and transform with <algorithm> and lambda functions.

slides.title: Don't write it yourself
slides.text:
`<algorithm>` and `<numeric>` contain dozens of tested algorithms:
`sort`, `find`, `count_if`, `max_element`, `reverse`, `accumulate`...
They work on **ranges**: `v.begin()` to `v.end()`.
slides.narration: Before writing a loop, check the algorithm header. It has tested, fast implementations of sorting, searching, counting and much more. They work on a range given by two iterators, begin and end.

slides.title: Sorting
slides.text: `std::sort` sorts ascending by default.
slides.narration: Std sort sorts a range in ascending order. Pass std greater to sort descending. It runs in n log n time.

slides.title: Lambdas
slides.text: A small function written inline.
slides.narration: A lambda is a function without a name, written right where you need it. Square brackets start it, then the parameters, then the body. Here a lambda tells count if which elements to count.

slides.title: Custom sort order
slides.text: Give `sort` a lambda that says when `a` comes before `b`.
slides.narration: You can sort by any rule. The comparison lambda returns true when the first argument should come before the second. Here we sort words by length, and alphabetically when lengths are equal.

slides.title: More useful algorithms
slides.text:
- `std::accumulate(b, e, 0)` sum
- `std::max_element(b, e)` iterator to the largest
- `std::find(b, e, x)` search
- `std::reverse(b, e)`
- `std::transform` apply to each
slides.narration: A few more favorites: accumulate sums a range, max element finds the largest, find searches for a value, reverse flips a range, and transform applies a function to every element.

quiz.q: What does v.end() refer to?
quiz.explain: Ranges are half-open: end is one past the last.

quiz.q: Which header provides std::accumulate?
quiz.explain: accumulate is in <numeric>.

quiz.q: What does [](int x) { return x > 0; } create?
quiz.explain: This is lambda syntax.

exercise.title: Sort by length
exercise.prompt:
Read `n`, then `n` words. Sort them by **length** (shortest first); words of equal length go in **alphabetical** order.
Print each word on its own line. Use `std::sort` with a lambda.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: Create your own types with data, member functions, constructors and encapsulation.

slides.title: Objects bundle data and behavior
slides.text:
A **class** describes a new type: its data (**members**) and what it can do (**member functions**).
An **object** is one value of that type.
slides.narration: Classes let you create your own types. A class combines data with the functions that work on that data. Each object you create from the class has its own copy of the data.

slides.title: A first class
slides.text: `private` data, `public` interface.
slides.narration: Here is a counter class. The count is private, so outside code cannot mess with it directly. The public functions are the only way in. This idea is called encapsulation.

slides.title: Constructors
slides.text: Set up a valid object when it is created.
slides.narration: A constructor runs when an object is created and makes sure it starts in a valid state. The member initializer list after the colon is the preferred way to set members.

slides.title: const member functions
slides.text: `const` after the parameters: this function does not change the object.
slides.narration: Mark member functions that only read data as const. You can then call them on const objects, and the compiler guarantees they do not modify anything.

slides.title: Protecting invariants
slides.text:
An **invariant** is a rule that must always hold:
- a balance is never negative
- a date has a valid month
Public functions check inputs so the rule can't break.
slides.narration: The real power of private data is protecting invariants, rules that must always be true. If the only way to change the balance is a withdraw function that checks the amount, the balance can never go negative.

slides.title: struct vs class
slides.text:
Both create types. The only difference: default access.
- `struct` members are **public** by default
- `class` members are **private** by default
Use `struct` for plain data, `class` when you protect invariants.
slides.narration: C plus plus has both struct and class. The only technical difference is that struct members are public by default. By convention, use struct for simple data bundles and class when you hide data behind an interface.

quiz.q: By default, members of a class are:
quiz.explain: class defaults to private; struct defaults to public.

quiz.q: What does const after a member function's parameter list mean?
options: It does not modify the object
quiz.explain: A const member function cannot change the object's members.

quiz.q: When does a constructor run?
options: When a member function is called
quiz.explain: Constructors initialize new objects.

exercise.title: Bank account
exercise.prompt:
Implement a `BankAccount` class with private balance (starting at 0), and member functions `deposit`, `withdraw` and `balance`.

Read commands until the end of input:
- `deposit X` - add X
- `withdraw X` - subtract X, but if X is larger than the balance, print `insufficient funds` and change nothing
- `balance` - print the current balance

tests.input:
deposit 50
withdraw 50
balance
deposit 7
withdraw 8
balance

lessons.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
lessons.summary: Model is-a relationships and call the right behavior through virtual functions.

slides.title: Inheritance
slides.text: A **derived** class extends a **base** class.
slides.narration: Inheritance lets a new class reuse and extend an existing one. A circle is a shape, so circle can inherit from shape. The derived class gets the public interface of the base.

slides.title: virtual and override
slides.text: Each derived class supplies its own version.
slides.narration: A virtual function can be replaced in derived classes. Write override on the replacement so the compiler checks that you really are overriding something. Equals zero makes the base function pure, so Shape cannot be created on its own.

slides.title: Polymorphism
slides.text: One interface, many behaviors.
slides.narration: Now the magic. Through a reference or pointer to Shape, calling area runs the correct version for the real object, circle or rectangle. Code can work with any shape without knowing its exact type.

slides.title: Owning many shapes
slides.text: Store `std::unique_ptr<Shape>` in a vector.
slides.narration: To keep different shapes in one container, store smart pointers to the base class. Make unique creates each object, and the memory is freed automatically.

slides.title: Rules of thumb
slides.text:
- A base class with virtual functions needs a **virtual destructor**
- Always write `override`
- Prefer **composition** ("has-a") unless it is truly "is-a"
slides.narration: Three rules of thumb. Give polymorphic base classes a virtual destructor. Always mark overrides. And do not overuse inheritance: often, having a member object is simpler than being a subclass.

quiz.q: What does override do?
options: Asks the compiler to check that the function overrides a virtual one
quiz.explain: override catches signature mistakes at compile time.

quiz.q: A class with a pure virtual function (= 0) is:
quiz.explain: Abstract classes serve as interfaces.

quiz.q: Why does a polymorphic base class need a virtual destructor?
options: So deleting through a base pointer destroys the derived object correctly
quiz.explain: Otherwise only the base part is destroyed.

exercise.title: Shape areas
exercise.prompt:
Create an abstract `Shape` with a virtual `area()`, and derived `Circle` and `Rect` classes.

Read shapes until the end of input. Each line is either `circle R` or `rect W H`.
Store them as `std::unique_ptr<Shape>` in a vector, then print each area with **2 decimals**, one per line, followed by a final line `total T` (also 2 decimals). Use pi = `std::acos(-1.0)`.

lessons.title: Templates and generic code
lessons.summary: Write one function or class that works for many types.

slides.title: The problem
slides.text:
`int max_of(int, int)`, `double max_of(double, double)`, `string max_of(...)`...
Same logic, copied for every type.
**Templates** write it once.
slides.narration: Imagine writing the same max function for ints, doubles and strings. The logic is identical, only the type changes. Templates let you write the code once and let the compiler generate each version.

slides.title: Function templates
slides.text: `T` is a placeholder for a type.
slides.narration: A function template starts with template and typename T. T stands for any type. When you call it with ints, the compiler creates an int version automatically.

slides.title: Templates over containers
slides.text: Generic code over a whole vector.
slides.narration: Templates shine with containers. This function finds the largest element of a vector of any type, as long as the type supports the less than operator.

slides.title: Class templates
slides.text: The STL itself is built from them.
slides.narration: Classes can be templates too. In fact, vector and map are class templates, which is why you write the element type in angle brackets. Here is a tiny generic pair of values.

slides.title: Concepts (C++20)
slides.text:
Constrain templates with readable requirements:
`template <std::integral T> T gcd(T a, T b);`
Wrong types give a **clear** error message.
slides.narration: In C plus plus twenty, concepts let you state what a template needs, such as an integral type. If someone uses the wrong type, they get a short, clear error instead of pages of messages.

quiz.q: What does typename T mean in template <typename T>?
options: T is a placeholder for a type
quiz.explain: T stands for any type supplied when the template is used.

quiz.q: std::vector<int> is an example of:
quiz.explain: vector is a class template; vector<int> is an instantiation.

quiz.q: Why are templates usually defined in header files?
options: The compiler needs the full definition where they are used
It is required by the OS
quiz.explain: Instantiation needs the template's full code.

exercise.title: Generic largest
exercise.prompt:
Write **one** template function `T largest(const std::vector<T>& v)` and use it twice.

Input: `n`, then `n` integers, then `m`, then `m` words.
Print the largest integer on the first line and the alphabetically largest word on the second line.

lessons.title: Streams, files and parsing
lessons.summary: Read and write files with fstream and parse text with stringstream.

slides.title: Everything is a stream
slides.text:
- `std::cin` / `std::cout` - console
- `std::ifstream` / `std::ofstream` - files
- `std::istringstream` - read from a string
Same `<<`, `>>` and `getline` everywhere.
slides.narration: C plus plus uses the same stream idea for the console, files and strings. Once you know arrows and getline, you can read and write any of them the same way.

slides.title: Writing a file
slides.text: `std::ofstream` opens a file for output.
slides.narration: To write a file, create an ofstream with the file name and use it exactly like cout. Check that it opened. When the stream goes out of scope, the file closes automatically.

slides.title: Reading a file
slides.text: `std::ifstream` + `getline` reads line by line.
slides.narration: To read, create an ifstream and loop with getline. The loop ends at the end of the file. No explicit close is needed, but you may call close when you are done early.

slides.title: Parsing with stringstream
slides.text: Split a line into fields.
slides.narration: To split a line into fields, wrap it in an istringstream. Getline with a third argument reads up to a separator, like a comma. This is how you parse simple CSV data.

slides.title: RAII: files close themselves
slides.text:
A stream object **owns** its file.
When the object is destroyed, the destructor closes the file.
No leaks, even if an error happens.
slides.narration: File streams are a great example of RAII, resource acquisition is initialization. The object owns the file, and its destructor closes it automatically, even if the function exits early because of an error.

quiz.q: Which class writes to a file?
quiz.explain: o for output: ofstream.

quiz.q: What does std::getline(ss, field, ',') do?
options: Reads up to the next comma
quiz.explain: The third argument is the delimiter.

quiz.q: When is an std::ofstream's file closed if you never call close()?
options: When the stream object is destroyed
quiz.explain: The destructor closes the file (RAII).

exercise.title: CSV report
exercise.prompt:
Each input line has the form `name,score` (score is an integer). Read lines until the end.
Use `std::istringstream` and `std::getline` with `','` to split each line.

Print:
- `best NAME` (the first student with the highest score)
- `total T`
- `average A` with 2 decimals

lessons.title: Modern C++: RAII, smart pointers and safety
lessons.summary: Write safe modern C++ with RAII, smart pointers, optional and good habits.

slides.title: RAII
slides.text:
**Resource Acquisition Is Initialization**
- a constructor acquires a resource (memory, file, lock)
- the destructor releases it
Cleanup becomes automatic and exception-safe.
slides.narration: RAII is the most important idea in modern C plus plus. Tie every resource to an object. The constructor acquires it and the destructor releases it, so cleanup happens automatically, even when errors occur.

slides.title: No raw new/delete
slides.text: Use containers and smart pointers instead.
slides.narration: Raw new and delete are easy to get wrong: forget delete and you leak, delete twice and you crash. Modern code almost never uses them. Unique pointer owns an object and deletes it automatically.

slides.title: unique_ptr and shared_ptr
slides.text:
- `std::unique_ptr` - **one** owner, cannot be copied, can be moved
- `std::shared_ptr` - shared ownership, counts owners
- Default to `unique_ptr`
slides.narration: Unique pointer has exactly one owner. You can move it but not copy it. Shared pointer allows several owners and frees the object when the last one is gone. Prefer unique pointer unless you truly need sharing.

slides.title: std::optional
slides.text: A value that may be missing - without magic numbers.
slides.narration: Sometimes a function might not have a result. Instead of returning minus one or a null pointer, return std optional. The caller must check whether a value is there.

slides.title: Move semantics
slides.text: Transfer resources instead of copying them.
slides.narration: Moving lets an object hand over its resources, like the buffer of a big vector, instead of copying them. Std move marks an object as ready to be moved from. Containers use moves automatically to stay fast.

slides.title: Professional habits
slides.text:
- compile with `-Wall -Wextra`, use sanitizers
- `const` by default, `auto` where clear
- prefer `std::vector`, `std::string`, algorithms
- follow the **C++ Core Guidelines**
slides.narration: Finally, some professional habits. Turn on warnings and sanitizers, make things const by default, prefer standard containers and algorithms, and read the C plus plus Core Guidelines.

quiz.q: What does RAII guarantee?
options: Resources are released automatically by destructors
quiz.explain: Resource lifetime is tied to object lifetime.

quiz.q: Which smart pointer should you use by default for single ownership?
quiz.explain: unique_ptr has no overhead and clear ownership.

quiz.q: What does std::optional<int> represent?
options: An int that may be absent
quiz.explain: optional either holds a value or is empty (std::nullopt).

exercise.title: Sum valid numbers
exercise.prompt:
Read tokens (separated by whitespace) until the end of input.
Write `std::optional<int> parse_int(const std::string&)` that accepts only tokens that are **entirely** a valid integer (use `std::from_chars`).

Print `sum=S invalid=K` where S is the sum of valid numbers and K counts invalid tokens.

lessons.title: Problem solving with the STL
lessons.summary: Turn slow brute force into fast solutions using hash maps, sorting and complexity thinking.

slides.title: A method for any problem
slides.text:
1. Restate the input and output precisely
2. Solve a small case by hand
3. Write the **brute force** idea
4. Find what is repeated, and speed it up
5. Test edge cases
slides.narration: Here is a method for any programming problem. Restate it, solve a small example by hand, write the simple brute force idea, then look for repeated work you can avoid. Finally, test the tricky cases.

slides.title: Complexity matters
slides.text:
For n = 100,000:
- O(n^2) -> 10 billion steps: **too slow**
- O(n log n) -> ~1.7 million: fast
- O(n) -> 100,000: instant
slides.narration: Complexity tells you if a solution is fast enough. With a hundred thousand items, a quadratic algorithm needs ten billion steps, far too slow. An n log n or linear algorithm finishes instantly.

slides.title: Two Sum: brute force
slides.text: Check every pair: O(n^2).
slides.narration: Classic problem: find two positions whose values add up to a target. The brute force way checks every pair with two loops. It works, but it is quadratic.

slides.title: Two Sum: hash map
slides.text: Remember what you've seen: O(n).
slides.narration: The fast way scans once. For each value, ask a hash map whether its complement, target minus the value, was seen before. Lookups are constant time on average, so the whole solution is linear.

slides.title: Your toolbox
slides.text:
- counting -> `unordered_map`
- unique / seen -> `unordered_set`
- ordering -> `sort`, `map`
- always the min/max -> `priority_queue`
- ranges of sums -> prefix sums
slides.narration: Here is your toolbox. Counting uses a hash map, seen before questions use a set, ordering uses sort or map, repeatedly taking the smallest or largest uses a priority queue, and range sums use prefix sums.

slides.title: Where next?
slides.text:
- Data structures and algorithms practice
- Build systems: **CMake**, testing with GoogleTest
- Concurrency: `std::thread`, `std::jthread`
- Graphics/games, embedded, high-performance computing
slides.narration: You have reached the end of the course, congratulations! Keep practicing algorithms, learn CMake and unit testing, and explore concurrency, games or high performance computing. C plus plus will take you far.

lessons.notes:
## From brute force to fast

Most efficient solutions come from one question: **what work am I repeating?**

| Problem | Brute force | Better |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| pair with given sum | O(n^2) pairs | O(n) hash map |
| duplicates | O(n^2) compare all | O(n) set or O(n log n) sort |
| range sums | O(n) per query | O(1) with prefix sums |
| k largest | sort O(n log n) | heap O(n log k) |

## Two Sum with a hash map

```cpp
std::unordered_map<int, int> firstIndex;
for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
    if (auto it = firstIndex.find(target - a[j]); it != firstIndex.end()) {
        std::cout << it->second << ' ' << j << '\n';
        return 0;
    }
    firstIndex.emplace(a[j], j);   // emplace does nothing if the key exists
}
std::cout << "none\n";
```

Because we look up **before** inserting `a[j]`, an element is never paired with itself.

## priority_queue

```cpp
std::priority_queue<int> pq;           // max-heap
std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>> minq;  // min-heap
```

## Testing your solution

- smallest input (n = 1 or 2)
- no answer exists
- duplicates and negative numbers
- the largest allowed input (is it fast?)

## Fast I/O tip

For large inputs, add at the start of `main`:
```cpp
std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
std::cin.tie(nullptr);
```

## Keep going

Practice on problem sites, read the C++ Core Guidelines, and build a real project with CMake and unit tests.

quiz.q: Average time of a lookup in std::unordered_map?
quiz.explain: Hash tables give constant time on average.

quiz.q: Roughly how many steps does an O(n^2) algorithm take for n = 100,000?
quiz.explain: 100,000 squared is 10^10.

quiz.q: In the hash map Two Sum, why look up before inserting a[j]?
options: So an element is never paired with itself
quiz.explain: Inserting first could match a[j] with itself when target = 2*a[j].

exercise.title: Two Sum
exercise.prompt:
Read `n`, then `n` integers `a[0..n-1]`, then a `target`.
Find indices `i < j` with `a[i] + a[j] == target`. Choose the pair with the **smallest j**; for that j, the **smallest i**.
Print `i j` (0-based), or `none` if no pair exists. Aim for O(n) with `std::unordered_map`.
